description: Moonle turns raw NASA lunar terrain and ephemeris data into landing-site decisions anyone can test. Browse any lunar coordinate and Moonle tells you how much sunlight the site gets, how long its longest night is, when Earth is in view, how big a battery you need, and which landing dates work.
summary:
Moonle is a landing-site navigator for the Moon’s south pole. We developed a data pipeline and web app that turn open NASA data, LOLA terrain elevation (240 m per pixel) and the JPL DE421 ephemeris, into decisions a mission planner can use. For each site, Moonle computes the terrain skyline and the hourly positions of the Sun and Earth over three years. It then adds engineering models that estimate solar power, battery survival and the Earth communications link. The results show how much sunlight a site gets, its longest night, when Earth is in view, the battery needed to survive, and which landing dates work if a launch slips. [Users can also test their own south-pole coordinates.]

This addresses the challenge by turning raw data into clear answers for choosing and comparing landing sites. It matters because the south pole is where future missions want to go, and picking a site there is slow and expert-only. Moonle makes that analysis faster, more accessible and open to check, with validation against JPL Horizons and stated limits.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?
Moonle is a landing-site navigator for the Moon’s south pole. It turns NASA terrain and ephemeris data into answers a mission planner can use: how much sunlight a site gets, its longest night, when Earth is in view, the battery needed to survive, and which landing dates work. Our engine builds each site’s terrain skyline from LOLA elevation data (240 m per pixel), combines it with hourly JPL DE421 Sun and Earth positions over 3 years, and feeds that into Python power, battery and comms models. [Users can also type in their own south-pole coordinate.]

What benefits does it have?
It makes expert-only data usable by anyone, quantifies design trade-offs (a ~354-hour equatorial night needs about 124 kg of battery, versus a few kg at a good polar ridge), and answers “my launch slipped, now what?” with good and bad landing dates. It also shows which sites need a relay satellite. Every number traces back to a named NASA dataset.

What is the intended impact?
We want to make landing-site screening faster and more accessible, and grow it into an open, validated atlas of south-pole lighting and communications that others can reuse and check.

What tools did you use?
Python (NumPy, Matplotlib, pytest), Git and GitHub. Data: NASA LRO/LOLA LDEM_75S_240M and the JPL DE421 ephemeris, validated against JPL Horizons and LROC Quickmap. No special hardware, we used Claude for drafting code, documentation and slides and reviewed the results ourselves.

How is it creative?
It is a data-to-decision pipeline, not just a map. It puts engineering numbers on the same screen as the geometry, shows why panel orientation matters at the pole (a flat panel is nearly useless, a vertical one is excellent), and tackles real scenarios like a slipped launch or a site with no view of Earth.

What factors did your team consider?
Accuracy (we validated against external references and state our limits: 240 m terrain, hourly sampling, simplified Sun disk), honest assumptions (representative hardware values, each documented with a source), sensitivity of the results, reproducibility, accessibility, and scope: with one weekend we focused on the south pole.
